title: Contextual micro-agent toolkit and runbook fragment router
creator: Aisha Romero
description:
Build a lightweight runtime and developer toolkit for composing, routing, and hot-patching small "runbook fragments" (micro-agents) used by internal support automation. Goal: enable on-call engineers to assemble targeted remediation flows from vetted fragments, route execution based on contextual predicates (cluster/region/tenant severity), and fallback safely to human-approved steps.

Scope and deliverables:
- A micro-agent format (YAML+typed inputs) with simple lifecycle hooks (validate, dry-run, apply, rollback).
- A fragment router service that evaluates predicates against request context and telemetry, selects a candidate sequence, and enforces RBAC & approval gating.
- Dry-run & simulated replay harness integrated with CI so fragments can be exercised against recorded trace snippets.
- Telemetry signals and intent scoring used to auto-suggest fragment sequences in the Console support UI.
- A patching workflow to hot-swap fragment implementations with canary and audit logs.

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
- Runtime complexity vs on-call velocity: we prefer minimal runtime semantics (no long-lived state) to keep failures visible and easy to reason about; heavy stateful orchestration remains in higher-level playbooks.
- Safety-first defaults: fragments run in a restricted sandbox by default; any fragment that requires elevated access must carry an approval policy. This increases friction for a few high-value quickfixes but drastically reduces blast radius.
- Fragment DSL vs ad-hoc scripts: choose a small, typed DSL (templated shell + typed params) rather than arbitrary scripts to enable static validation, input schema checks, and safer replay.

Open questions:
- Should the router support ML-based ranking of fragments (telemetry-driven) in v1 or defer to rule-based heuristics? (current plan: rule-based first, ML ranking as an experiment).
- How granular should fragment-level audit logs be for ease of debugging without overwhelming the observability pipeline?
